title: Ranges Holding the Top Value K Times
statement:
You get an array nums and an integer k. Let top be the largest value in the whole array.

Count the contiguous subarrays in which top appears at least k times. Two subarrays count separately if they start or end at different positions, even when they hold the same values.

Note that top is fixed by the whole array. A subarray whose own largest value is smaller than top never counts.

examples.why: top = 5, at indexes 1, 3 and 4. Ending at index 3 there are 2 valid starts (0 and 1); ending at index 4 there are 4 (0 to 3). 2 + 4 = 6.
top is 7 and appears only once. The subarray [1, 1] has its own maximum twice, but that maximum is not 7.
Every one of the 6 subarrays contains at least one 3.

hints: Fix where the subarray ends. Which starting positions work?
If a window [l, r] already holds k copies of top, then every window [l', r] with l' ≤ l holds them too. So the valid starts for a given end form a prefix 0..something.
Slide a window: add nums[r], and while the window holds k copies of top, drop nums[l] and move l right. After that, exactly l starts (0 to l − 1) were valid for this end.

explain.intuition:
Fix the right end r. Moving the start further left only adds elements, so it can only add copies of top. That means the valid starts for this end are always a block 0, 1, …, p: once a start works, every earlier start works too.

A sliding window finds p for every end at once. Grow the window to the right. Whenever it holds k copies, shrink it from the left until it holds k − 1. Every start you shrank past was a valid start for this end, so after shrinking, l itself is the number of valid starts. And because the right end only grows, l never needs to move back.
steps: Find top, the largest value of the array.
Keep l = 0, seen = 0 (copies of top inside the window) and total = 0.
While seen ≥ k: if nums[l] === top, decrease seen; move l right.
Add l to total. It counts the starts 0 to l − 1, each of which gives a valid subarray ending at r.
pitfalls: Using the maximum of each subarray instead of the maximum of the whole array. In [1, 1, 7] with k = 2 the answer is 0.
Counting only the shortest valid window for each end (adding 1 instead of l). Every longer window to the left is valid too.
Storing the total in a 32-bit integer. With 100 000 equal values the count is about 5·10⁹.

solutions.title: Every start, extend to the right
solutions.idea: For each start, walk right and count copies of top. Once the count reaches k, every longer end works too, so add them all and stop.

solutions.title: Sliding window, count the starts
solutions.idea: Shrink the window until it holds fewer than k copies of top. Every start the left pointer passed is valid for the current end, so add l.

followups: Count the subarrays where top appears exactly k times. (Hint: at least k minus at least k + 1.)
Solve it by storing the positions of top and, for each end, looking up the k-th most recent one. When is that clearer than the window?
lcTitle: Count Subarrays Where Max Element Appears at Least K Times
